item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are hoping to get one of their key bats back before the calendar flips to October.
Contreras' Injury and Recovery Timeline
Willson Contreras has been dealing with a hand injury after getting hit by a pitch on his right hand earlier in the week in Texas, an injury that's still visibly swollen and bruised days later. According to Peter Abraham of the Boston Globe, Contreras showed reporters the spot on his knuckles where the pitch connected. "When I got hit, I felt my hand going numb. I thought it was bad because that's a sign of a fracture," Contreras said. "That's why I came off the game."
Initial X-rays came back negative, though further imaging is being held off until the swelling subsides. Contreras sounds confident there's no fracture, drawing on past experience with broken bones to gauge the severity this time around.
The first baseman is hoping to take swings as soon as Sunday, though the nature of the injury complicates things given it's on his top hand, the one that absorbs the shock of contact. He's even considered wearing a protective guard over his batting glove if he does return. With Boston off Monday and playing the Rays again Sunday, Tuesday's game against the Guardians looks like the most realistic target for a potential comeback. "I'm going to take it day-to-day. Of course I want to come back and play with the guys and be there for them," Contreras said. "It's a part of baseball."
Contreras has now been hit by a pitch 24 times this season, tied for third-most in the majors, and 47 times across the last two seasons combined. Much of that stems from how close he stands to the plate, and he's voiced frustration about the pattern, at one point suggesting Boston's pitching staff should retaliate on his behalf.
Willson Contreras has more range of motion when he squeezes his hand today than he did yesterday. It remains a day to day monitoring for improvement. He is fairly confident it isn't fractured. He will do everything he can to play through this once symptoms allow.
— Ian Browne (@IanMBrowne) September 19, 2026
Other Red Sox Injury News
Contreras isn't the only Red Sox player working his way back. Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela has been out since Sept. 3 with a strained right quadriceps. He faced live pitching for the first time since the injury during a Saturday workout in Worcester. "I felt comfortable," Rafaela said. He still needs to test a full-effort sprint before he's cleared. He plans to attempt that Sunday, with a possible return targeted for Tuesday against Cleveland.
On the pitching side, Tanner Houck continued his rehab from elbow surgery. He worked 3.1 innings in a minor league outing that included two strikeouts and no walks. It was his fourth appearance in that process. He could factor into Boston's bullpen plans for the postseason. Left-hander Garrett Crochet hasn't pitched since April 25 due to shoulder inflammation. He's targeting live hitters early this week, likely at Fenway Park. Whether that's enough to earn a postseason roster spot remains unclear. Right-handed reliever Tyron Guerrero could be activated as soon as Sunday after being out since Sept. 1 with a sore shoulder.

item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

Sep 20, 2026, 12:47 AM ET
WEEI's Rob Bradford reports that it is "sure looking like" Boston Red Sox left-hander Payton Tolle has a "good shot" at pitching Game 1 of a wild-card series to kick off the postseason with the way the Red Sox are lining things up. It means that the 23-year-old southpaw will not get a start this weekend against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays. The former second-rounder from TCU in 2024 has had a strong first full season in the big leagues with Boston in 2026, going 9-6 with a 3.02 ERA (3.04 FIP) and 1.07 WHIP with 166 strikeouts and 38 walks in 143 innings across his 25 starts. Another lefty, Patrick Sandoval, is now scheduled to make the start for the BoSox in the series finale in Tampa. Tolle allowed four earned runs in 5 2/3 innings against the Seattle Mariners on Aug. 31, but he has only given up one earned run with one walk and 19 punchouts in 12 innings across his last two starts against the Baltimore Orioles and Kansas City Royals in September.--Keith Hernandez
Source: WEEI - Rob Bradford
More Recent News
Xavier Edwards Leaves Early on Saturday With Thumb Discomfort


Keith Hernandez




Sep 20, 2026, 12:31 AM ET
Miami Marlins infielder Xavier Edwards (thumb) left Saturday night's game at Petco Park against the San Diego Padres early with discomfort in his left thumb, according to Christina De Nicola. The Marlins' training staff was checking Edwards' left hand out when he fouled a ball off in the seventh frame. It is worth noting that Edwards previously missed time this season with a sprained left thumb, which he might have aggravated on Saturday night. Before leaving the ballgame, Edwards went 0-for-3 with a walk and two strikeouts. He was replaced at the keystone in San Diego by Jared Serna. If the 27-year-old switch-hitting middle infielder did aggravate his left-thumb sprain, there is a good chance that he will not play again for the Marlins in the final week of the 2026 season. Edwards came into Wednesday's contest with a nice .282/.361/.373 slash line with a .733 OPS, a career-high six home runs, a career-high 52 RBI, 61 runs scored, and 21 stolen bases in 141 games played. He has stolen 20-plus bases in each of the last three seasons, including a career-high 31 back in 2024.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Christina De Nicola
Aaron Judge Hopes to be Back for Postseason, No Timetable Given


Keith Hernandez




Sep 20, 2026, 12:23 AM ET
New York Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge (calf) said on Saturday that his right-calf strain is in the soleus muscle, according to Bryan Hoch of MLB.com. However, Judge would not say what grade of strain his MRI exam revealed. "I'd like to be back by the postseason. That's definitely the plan. I got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that," Judge said. The New York Daily News' Gary Phillips reports that neither Judge nor manager Aaron Boone has shared much information on his injury, with the Yankees treating his calf strain like "classified CIA intel." "It doesn't matter what grade it is," Boone said. "We're at nine games left [in the season]." Because we have no idea of the exact severity of his calf injury, it is entirely plausible that Judge could miss most, or all, of any potential Yankees playoff run in October. Judge has been throwing, working out, and getting treatment, and he said he is "gonna do everything we can do to get back as soon as we can." Boone, though, merely said he is "hoping for the best." It will be difficult for the Yankees to go all the way if they do not get Judge back for the playoffs. It has been a frustrating year for the three-time MVP and all of his fantasy managers, as he has only played in 66 games due to a stress fracture in his rib, slashing .241/.360/.511 with 18 home runs, 41 RBI, 45 runs, and five steals.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Bryan Hoch
Roki Sasaki to Return Next Week


Andy Webb




Sep 19, 2026, 10:37 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Roki Sasaki (finger) will make his return to the mound next week during the series against the San Diego Padres, David Vassegh reports. Sasaki looked good during his side session on Wednesday, so the Dodgers have cleared him to get back on the mound. It doesn't sound like the Dodgers have decided whether Sasaki will start or come out of the bullpen during his outing against the Padres. The right-hander has been out since late August due to a finger blister. The expectation is that Sasaki will likely pitch in a bullpen role for the team during the postseason.--Andy Webb
Source: David Vassegh
Trey Yesavage to Start on Monday


Andy Webb




Sep 19, 2026, 10:31 PM ET
Toronto Blue Jays starting pitcher Trey Yesavage (knee) is scheduled to start against the Baltimore Orioles on Monday, Arden Zwelling of Sportsnet.ca reports. Yesavage has been out since August after having surgery to repair a torn meniscus in his right knee. He only made one rehab appearance at Triple-A Buffalo before getting cleared to pitch for the big league club. The Jays plan to have Yesavage pitch roughly three innings or around 45 to 50 pitches. Spencer Miles is expected to take over for the bulk of the innings after Yesavage is done. It'll be interesting to see if the Jays decide to shut down Yesavage if they do get eliminated from playoff contention. Until then, it sounds like the right-hander is going to contribute here soon.--Andy Webb
Source: Arden Zwelling
Cal Quantrill Removed with Lat Tightness


Andy Webb




Sep 19, 2026, 10:22 PM ET
Texas Rangers starting pitcher Cal Quantrill (lat) exited early during Saturday's outing against the Toronto Blue Jays. Quantrill was pulled out in the second inning due to right lat tightness, Kennedi Landry of MLB.com reports. He was able to record four outs before exiting this contest. Jordan Montgomery took over on the mound and threw 3.2 scoreless innings. Quantrill figures to undergo an MRI, so fantasy managers will likely have to wait for the results on that. Nathan Eovaldi could be asked to move back into the starting rotation if Quantrill is forced to miss time. UPDATE: The Dallas Morning News' Shawn McFarland reports that Quantrill will undergo an MRI exam on Sunday morning, per manager Skip Schumaker.--Andy Webb
Source: Kennedi Landry
Sep 19, 2026, 10:15 PM ET
New York Yankees outfielder Spencer Jones (foot) was not in the starting lineup ahead of Saturday's game against the Arizona Diamondbacks. The Yankees decided to rest Jones on Saturday due to left foot/heel soreness, according to Brendan Kuty of The Athletic. It sounds like a day-to-day issue, so the Yankees are just going to play it safe. Jones is 1-for-19 with nine strikeouts over his last four games, so he could probably use a day off to rest and reset. Jose Caballero takes over in center field for Saturday's game. Fantasy managers should check back ahead of Sunday's game for another update on Jones.--Andy Webb
Source: Brendan Kuty
Shohei Ohtani Takes Simulated At-Bats


Andy Webb




Sep 19, 2026, 10:05 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers two-way superstar Shohei Ohtani (knee, biceps) has progressed to taking simulated at-bats off the team's pitching machine on Saturday, Jack Harris of the California Post reports. Ohtani was also able to run the bases as he works his way back from a biceps and knee issue. It's unclear if Ohtani will return when he's first eligible on Wednesday. The Dodgers have already clinched the postseason, so they don't exactly need to rush him back into the lineup. However, the Dodgers would probably like for Ohtani to play in a few regular-season games before the playoffs begin. Fantasy managers should check back for another update in a few days.--Andy Webb
Source: Jack Harris
Jac Caglianone Returning to Saturday's Lineup


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 5:54 PM ET
Kansas City Royals first baseman/outfielder Jac Caglianone (hand) is serving as the designated hitter and is batting third in Saturday's contest on the road against the Pittsburgh Pirates and right-hander Bubba Chandler, per MLB.com. Caglianone suffered a minor hand injury before Friday's series opener at PNC Park, but he is back in action on Saturday and should be returned to fantasy lineups against a right-hander, despite his cold streak of late. The 23-year-old former first-rounder has produced a .277/.328/.483 slash line with an .811 OPS, 23 home runs, 70 RBI, 66 runs scored, and six stolen bases in 484 at-bats in 2026 in his first full big-league season with the Royals. Cags was red-hot in August, slashing .411/.429/.684 with a 1.113 OPS, six home runs, eight doubles, 26 RBI, 17 runs scored, and three stolen bases in 24 games, but he has been banged up in September and has gone just 4-for-27 (.148) with zero homers, four RBI, one walk, and 11 strikeouts. He has never faced Chandler in the majors.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Sebastian Walcott to be Promoted to Triple-A


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 3:01 PM ET
Texas Rangers top infield prospect Sebastian Walcott is expected to be promoted to Triple-A Round Rock on Saturday, according to Kennedi Landry of MLB.com. Walcott will make his debut as the designated hitter on Saturday night. The No. 9 overall prospect in all of baseball, per MLB Pipeline, has only played in 39 games in the minors this year after having surgery on his UCL, but since returning, he has slashed .322/.398/.586 with nine home runs and 11 stolen bases in 37 games for Double-A Frisco. In a playoff series with the Rough Riders, Walcott went 4-for-11 with a homer and four stolen bases. Walcott is only 20 years old, but if he continues to ascend and looks good in spring training next year, he could push for an early-season MLB promotion for the Rangers. It is impossible to ignore his 40-homer upside at the shortstop position in fantasy baseball, which makes him a must-stash already in dynasty/keeper leagues.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Kennedi Landry
Orioles Shutting Ryan Helsley Down


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 1:40 PM ET
The Baltimore Orioles are shutting down right-handed reliever Ryan Helsley (elbow) for the rest of the season, general manager Mike Elias told Andy Kostka of The Baltimore Banner. The focus is on Helsley getting ready for next season. Elias said that Helsley is not dealing with a new injury, but the debate was over contracting his buildup timeline, and the O's opted against that. In related news, the Orioles reinstated right-handed reliever Felix Bautista (shoulder) from the 60-day injured list, and he will join the team's active roster for the first time since July of last year after he had surgery to fix a torn labrum and rotator cuff in his shoulder. Helsley's first year in Baltimore was a lost cause due to his elbow issues, as he was able to throw only 15 1/3 innings, going 0-4 with a 4.11 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 21 strikeouts, and eight saves in 17 appearances. He will not be a lock to open the 2027 campaign as Baltimore's primary closer, especially with Bautista now back and healthy.--Keith Hernandez
Source: The Baltimore Banner - Andy Kostka
Willson Contreras Still Out on Saturday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 1:04 PM ET
Boston Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras (hand) remains out of the team's starting lineup for Saturday's contest against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays for the second straight day, per MLB.com. Nick Sogard will make another start at first base and will bat fifth against Rays right-hander Freddy Peralta. Contreras was diagnosed with a bruised right hand after leaving Thursday's game against the Texas Rangers after he was hit by a pitch. X-rays came back negative, though, so he is considered day-to-day and could make his return in Sunday's series finale in Tampa. Fantasy managers are hoping to get the 34-year-old Venezuelan back in their starting lineups as soon as possible, as the four-time All-Star has hit a career-high 27 home runs while driving in 81 runs in 129 games and 533 plate appearances in his first year with the club. Various injuries have limited Contreras to only four games so far in September, though, and he has gone 4-for-12 with a homer and two RBI.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Aroldis Chapman Won't Pitch This Weekend


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 11:07 AM ET
Boston Red Sox left-handed closer Aroldis Chapman (lat) felt some tightness in his lat while working out before Tuesday's game against the Texas Rangers and has not pitched since. Chapman said that he will not pitch this weekend against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays, but he expects to return during the final homestand of the regular season, which starts on Tuesday, according to Ian Browne of MLB.com. The veteran southpaw downplayed the injury on Friday, saying that the Red Sox are being conservative and that he felt healthy enough to play catch before the series opener against the Rays, but the team told him not to. "I'm not worried at all," Chapman said. "From the first time I felt it to today, I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time." Fantasy managers will be without Chapman this weekend, but for championship matchups next week, he will hopefully be ready to return to ninth-inning duties. The 38-year-old has been excellent in 2026 in his second year in Boston, posting a 1.95 ERA with a 1.14 WHIP, 34 saves, and 68 strikeouts in 50 2/3 innings pitched. Right-hander Garrett Whitlock should handle a save situation this weekend if it arises in Tampa.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Ian Browne
Justin Verlander Throws Live Batting Practice


Dave Funnell




Sep 19, 2026, 10:03 AM ET
Detroit Tigers starting pitcher Justin Verlander (hamstring/hip) threw a one-inning, 20-pitch live batting practice session on Friday. The 43-year-old said that he felt great after this successful outing. This was yet another step in the right direction, as it was his first time throwing against live batters. What lies ahead in his progress remains to be seen, as the plan is for him to pitch one final time in his illustrious career on Saturday, September 26, against the Pittsburgh Pirates. Whether or not he is able to throw one inning or more remains questionable, but with him retiring after this season, chances are he will be healthy enough to make that appearance and cap off one of baseball's greatest careers. With 266 wins and 3,554 strikeouts over 21 seasons, the surefire Hall of Famer will be looking to finish his career where it started: in Detroit.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller
Source: Chris McCosky
Trent Grisham Could Return This Season


Dave Funnell




Sep 19, 2026, 9:56 AM ET
New York Yankees outfielder Trent Grisham (hamstring) is pretty far into his recovery, two weeks after being placed on the 10-Day Injured List with a Grade 2 hamstring strain. Manager Aaron Boone reiterated that a return for him "could be in play" for the latter part of the season. It was also mentioned that when he does return, the Yankees would need to decide between him and Spencer Jones to play center field. This could complicate things for both players, as there could be some sort of platoon involving the two, diminishing their fantasy value down the stretch. Either way, the Yankees will be looking to solidify their lineup for the playoffs, and Grisham's fantasy value is very limited down the stretch, with or without a return before the playoffs.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller
Source: Brendan Kuty - The Athletic
Tristan Peters Dealing With Multiple Injuries


Dave Funnell




Sep 19, 2026, 9:39 AM ET
Chicago White Sox outfielder Tristan Peters (rib/shoulder) crashed into the wall during Friday's game while trying to catch a fly ball in the outfield. He exited the game with contusions to both his ribs and shoulders, and Braden Montgomery took his place in the outfield. The good news is that he is listed as day-to-day and has no head injury, which was the initial concern at the time of impact. It's unclear if he will miss any time before returning, but with the White Sox in the middle of a divisional race, they may need his help sooner rather than later. The 26-year-old is hitting .272 on the season with 12 home runs and eight stolen bases, and is worth rostering in deep leagues.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller
Source: Chicago White Sox
Justin Steele Completes Two-Inning Rehab Outing


Dave Funnell




Sep 19, 2026, 9:30 AM ET
Chicago Cubs pitcher Justin Steele (elbow) threw a 33-pitch, two-inning rehab outing on Friday for the Triple-A Iowa Cubs. This was his fifth appearance since beginning his rehab assignment and the fourth that has been two innings in length. Arguably his most impressive outing yet, Steele walked the first batter of the game before striking out the side. He would finish with five strikeouts in total while not allowing a hit. While the velocity on his fastball sat at 90.2 miles per hour, it was his slider that impressed the most, generating four whiffs. It's unclear what lies ahead for him, as the Cubs are in the middle of a race for the Wild Card. While they have a comfortable lead on the teams chasing them, they do need to prepare for the postseason, and Steele returning to the Cubs may not be in the cards. What's clear is that he is feeling much better than he has in quite some time, and any return to the Cubs would likely be for a peace-of-mind appearance to allow him to enter the postseason on a healthy note, giving him the opportunity to work on coming back even stronger next spring. Fantasy managers should not expect much from him down the stretch, but those in dynasty leagues should take note and add him while they can.--Dave Funnell - RotoBaller
Source: Jason Kempf
Bryce Eldridge Expected to Play on Saturday


Dave Funnell




Sep 19, 2026, 9:17 AM ET
San Francisco Giants first baseman Bryce Eldridge (head) was scratched from the lineup on Friday after cutting his head at the team's hotel before opening pitch. Manager Tony Vitello said that he expects the 21-year-old slugger to play on Saturday, noting that the injury doesn't appear to have any long-term ramifications. ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Willson Contreras stood at his locker Saturday afternoon and showed reporters the spot where a pitch hit his right hand in Texas on Thursday.
It was on the knuckles between his pinky finger and ring finger, and there was still swelling and a yellow bruise. Contreras could flex his hand but can’t yet grip a bat well enough to hit.
If you didn’t know Contreras was a baseball player, you’d think he was a boxer based on his battered hands.
“When I got hit, I felt my hand going numb. I thought it was bad because that’s a sign of a fracture,” he said. “That’s why I came off the game.”
Contreras is hopeful of getting in a few games before the start of the postseason.
“Hand’s still really sore. Woke up feeling a little better,” he said. “I can squeeze a little better than [Friday], but it’s gonna take a few days.”
The initial X-rays were negative, and any further scans will wait until after the swelling goes down, but Contreras is confident there isn’t a fracture based on his experience.
“I can squeeze a lot better. I’ve had fractures before, and when I have fractures, I couldn’t squeeze,” he said.
Contreras is hoping he can take some swings on Sunday. But because the injury is to his top hand, he has to make sure he can absorb the impact of making contact.
“I’m going to take it day-to-day. Of course I want to come back and play with the guys and be there for them,” he said. “It’s a part of baseball.”
Contreras said he might try using a guard over his batting glove to protect his hand.
The Sox play the Rays on Sunday afternoon and are off on Monday. Contreras could possibly return on Tuesday against the Guardians.
“I’m going to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs,” he said.
Contreras has been hit 24 times this season, tied for third-most in the majors, and 47 times over last two seasons. It’s largely because he stands close to the plate. But Contreras suggested on Thursday that Sox pitchers should retaliate on his behalf.
“I see, and completely feel and understand Willson’s frustration,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “He’s been hit close to 50 times the last couple of years so he’s frustrated. Whether he’s referring to the umpires doing something or the pitchers, it’s irrelevant.”
Tracy acknowledged that Contreras crowds the plate. “But there’s a lot of guys that are close to the plate that don’t get hit as much as he does,” he said.
Rafaela progressing
Ceddanne Rafaela, who has been on the injured list since Sept. 3 with a strained right quadriceps, worked out at Worcester on Saturday and faced live pitching for the first time since the injury.
“I felt comfortable,” he said. “My body is rested, and I feel ready to go.”
The last hurdle is to sprint at 100 percent effort, something he will try on Sunday. Rafaela hopes to play against the Guardians on Tuesday.
Crochet could face hitters
Tracy said the goal set for Garrett Crochet would be to face hitters early in the week. That would likely be at Fenway Park before a game. Whether one such session would be enough to merit inclusion on the postseason roster isn’t certain. “Hard to say. I know that’s not a great answer, but it just really is,” Tracy said. … Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero could be activated off the injured list as soon as Sunday. He has been out since Sept. 1 with a sore shoulder.
Globe staff writer Alex Speier contributed to this report from Worcester.

On the verge of clinching a postseason berth for the second straight year, the Boston Red Sox have reason to be cautiously optimistic about the health of one of their best hitters.
Though still “pretty sore” from taking a pitch to the right hand on Sept. 17, Willson Contreras no longer believes he suffered a fracture, because he woke up feeling better and had improved range of motion and grip.
“I’m not concerned about having a fracture, just because I can squeeze a lot better today,” the All-Star first baseman told reporters before the team’s Saturday afternoon game at the Tampa Bay Rays’ Tropicana Field. “I had a fracture in my right hand in 2024 by hit-by-pitch, and I couldn’t squeeze at all.”
“But it’s going to take days,” Contreras cautioned.
Contreras’ 24th hit-by-pitch of the season, a 92.3 mph sinker from Rangers’ Jakob Junis to his knuckle in the eighth inning, was a moment of extreme panic for him and the team. Contreras initially went to take his base, but was evidently in severe pain and interim manager Chad Tracy and athletic trainer Dave Herrera quickly removed him from the game.
Though initial imaging was negative, Contreras and Tracy both acknowledged the swelling could be obscurative, with the former telling reporters postgame, “It felt like a fracture.”
“When I got hit, I felt my hand going numb, and I thought it was bad, because that’s a sign of a fracture,” Contreras said on Saturday. “And it was like, tingling for like five minutes.”
Contreras will try to grip a bat on Sunday, and if so, try to do some cage work. He is champing at the bit to get back in games before the postseason begins. He has soared to new heights in his 11th big-league season and first with the Red Sox, putting up career-best marks in his .905 OPS, 59 walks, 81 RBI, and 27 home runs (129 games).
“I’m dying to go out and play with the guys and be there for them,” Contreras said. “It’s part of baseball; I’ll do everything in my power to get back on the field.”
“You don’t want to get to the playoffs without playing any games,” he said. “I want to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs. If it happens, it happens. If it doesn’t happen, we’ll see what happens.”
Contreras is one of several injured stars the Red Sox are eager to have back as they careen toward October baseball. Gold Glove centerfielder Ceddanne Rafaela last played Sept. 2 before going on the injured list with a right quad strain. Though it’s unlikely Rafaela will get into a Triple-A Worcester game before their season ends on Sunday, interim manager Chad Tracy described him as “moving quickly in the right direction,” and said the goal is for him to get “live BP-type at-bats of some kind, plus the Trajekt (pitching machine).”
All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman is not on the IL, but remains day-to-day due to the lat tightness he felt during a workout before Tuesday’s game in Texas. Though unavailable for this weekend’s series in Tampa, he told reporters there (through a team translator), “I’m not worried at all. … I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time.” Chapman plans to get back in games during the team’s final homestand, which begins Tuesday versus the Cleveland Guardians.

The Boston Red Sox could punch their ticket to the playoffs on Saturday, but health remains a bigger story with this club than the mechanics of a clinching scenario.
Ironically, as the Red Sox look to be locked into a first-round matchup against the New York Yankees, both archrivals are missing their best hitters. The Yankees placed Aaron Judge on the 10-day injured list with a calf strain on Friday, but the Red Sox are still waiting for clarity about Willson Contreras.
On Saturday, we learned that Contreras is at least somewhat on the mend after wearing a pitch to the left hand during Thursday night's game with the Texas Rangers. That's no guarantee of any time frame for a comeback, but it's definitely something positive to take from the day.
Latest update on Contreras sounds promising
According to Red Sox insider Ian Browne of MLB.com, Contreras saw an improvement in his condition from Friday to Saturday. That wasn't a guarantee that his hand avoided a fracture on the hit-by-pitch during Thursday's eighth inning, but Contreras sent a positive indication in that regard as well.
"Willson Contreras has more range of motion when he squeezes his hand today than he did yesterday," wrote Browne. "It remains a day to day monitoring for improvement. He is fairly confident it isn't fractured. He will do everything he can to play through this once symptoms allow."
Contreras homered on Tuesday in the series opener against Texas, giving him a career-high 27 on the season despite missing two weeks on the injured list at the start of this month. He's been the best hitter on the team by a wide margin, and ranks third among position players on the club with 4.6 bWAR.
It would be a big, big deal for the Red Sox to get Contreras not only back in time for that Yankees series in the Bronx, but to have a game or two in the regular season to tune him up. But it's still too early to know much of anything, and at this time of year, that's cause for plenty of nerves.

Quedó a un pelotazo de igualar el récord para venezolanos en una temporada.
El carabobeño Willson Contreras, de los Medias Rojas de Boston, se vio obligado a salir del encuentro del jueves contra los Rangers de Texas debido a un bolazo en la mano derecha, durante el octavo inning, en la victoria de su club 4-3.

Su compatriota Wilyer Abreu negoció un boleto para iniciar el episodio antes de que Contreras fuera golpeado por un sinker de 92.3 millas por hora (mph) de Jakob Junis.
El toletero de 34 años de edad, quien disputa su undécima campaña en las Grandes Ligas, cayó al suelo del dolor antes de pararse otra vez y dirigirse a la primera base, donde Abreu lo atendió brevemente. El mánager interino de los patirrojos, Chad Tracy, y los preparadores físicos entraron al terreno, y Willson Contreras salió del encuentro poco después.
Esta campaña el ahora inicialista lleva 24 pelotazos para igualar su tope personal del certamen de 2022.
El récord de número pelotazos para venezolanos en una temporada es de 25. Lo comparten el caraqueño Andrés Galarraga (1998) y el larense Andrés Giménez (2022).
Andrés Galarraga es el líder en pelotazos recibidos en la historia entre los criollos tras ser golpeado 178 veces en 19 temporadas y 2.257 partidos. A Willson Contreras le han pegado 153 pelotazos en 1.207 juegos.
Contreras ha alcanzado marcas personales en jonrones (27), impulsadas (81) y OPS+ (155) en su primera temporada con los Medias Rojas. Lleva 199 cuadrangulares por vida en MLB.
Las radiografías realizadas el jueves a la mano lesionada del carabobeño descartaron cualquier fractura.
Willson Contreras batea para promedio este año de .276 en 129 careos. El nativo de Puerto Cabello marcha líder jonronero e impulsor de Boston.

"At this point with (the Rays), we've played them enough already," Tracy said. "We have a pretty good understanding of them, (and) they have a pretty good understanding of us. But you could always pick up more stuff."
In Friday's series opener, the Red Sox scored four runs over the first three innings and won 4-2 to snap Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak and improve to 6-5 this season vs. the Rays.
Boston currently holds the second wild-card position in the American League but is dealing with several injuries.
"We have guys beat up that aren't here, and the hope is we get people healthy, and the roster could look even different a week from now than it does right now," Tracy said.
Boston's Willson Contreras is day-to-day after getting hit on the hand, while closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) has been unavailable the past two contests.
Right-hander Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery in 2025) and lefty Garrett Crochet (left shoulder inflammation) have advanced in their rehab assignments.
Boston left-hander Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.02 ERA) is expected to make his 26th start on Saturday and will try to record his sixth consecutive win.
Tolle is 1-0 with an 0.75 ERA over 12 innings in his last two starts, allowing one run on eight hits while striking out 19 with a walk. He is 0-2 with a 4.50 ERA in two starts and one relief outing against Tampa Bay, which already has clinched a playoff berth.
Whatever Rays pitching coach Kyle Snyder and the rest of the staff have done with trade-deadline acquisition Freddy Peralta certainly has been a success.
Acquired by the club from the New York Mets for three prospects on Aug. 2, Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) -- a right-hander who will start for the Rays on Saturday -- arrived from the Big Apple as a lesser version of what he was during his two All-Star seasons with the Milwaukee Brewers.
He was 5-9 with a 4.99 ERA with the Mets, but the work was immediately put in by the Rays to adjust Peralta to where he was when he was a 17-game winner with a sub-3.00 ERA last season.
"For some reason, when I got here, when I sat here with Kyle and (bullpen coach Jorge Moncada) and (manager Kevin Cash), they told me, like, 'You're gonna do what you want to do here, and we are going to help you to do it,'" Peralta said.
"And we know what you need to do to make those adjustments. We just put everything on the table. I just followed all the instructions, and it's what I am right now."
With the Rays, Peralta is 4-2 with a 3.86 ERA in eight starts, but his past four outings have been gems. He has pitched 23 innings and has allowed just two runs on 10 hits, with 17 strikeouts, four walks and an 0.78 ERA in that span.
"Fastball Freddy," who is using his changeup much more with the Rays, is 0-2 with a 5.40 ERA in three career starts against Boston.
Peralta allowed two runs on three hits in 4 1/3 innings in a 4-0 loss at Boston on July 11 while with the Mets.

The ever-fiery Willson Contreras had some on-brand quotes after his latest hit-by-pitch.
The Red Sox first baseman got drilled on the right hand by a pitch from Texas Rangers right-handed pitcher Jakob Junis in the eighth inning on Thursday night. He was in visible pain and immediately exited the game.
After the game, he said he thought his hand was fractured upon being struck, but he appears to have avoided serious injury. His X-rays came back negative.
Also postgame, Contreras expressed immense discontent with the fact that he’s been hit by pitches on 24 separate occasions this season. The total ties a career high (2022 with the Chicago Cubs) and continues a trend he’s experienced his entire MLB career. Only two players have been hit more this year (Cardinals’ Ivan Herrera, 29; White Sox’ Sam Antonacci, 27).
“I feel like … ” Contreras said, pausing for seven seconds, “I want to say something I can’t say. Let’s leave it at that (via The Boston Globe’s Tim Healey).”
Contreras, attempting to elaborate without getting into specifics, added:
“If nobody does anything about it, I’m going to keep getting hit. That’s the way I see it. That’s it.”
The 34-year-old, who has been Boston’s best hitter during its memorable season, came off the injured list last weekend after recovering from a hamstring strain. He expressed frustration about not knowing when he’ll return to the diamond again.
“It’s really frustrating because I just came back from the IL, and this might take days,” Contreras said. “I mean, sore bones in the hands — might take two days, might take a week, might take 10 days.”
Contreras is known as a right-handed batter who crowds the plate, which leads to more HBPs. He pushed back on that notion, though, saying other hitters do the same thing but get drilled less often.
“A lot of people might say that I hit on top of the plate, but I’m seeing a lot of players hit on top of the plate. They don’t get hit like me,” Contreras said.
The Venezuelan has been hit 146 times since 2018, which leads MLB.
Interim manager Chad Tracy offered an injury update on Contreras before Friday’s game against the Rays in Tampa.
“(He’s) sore. Obviously sore with some swelling,” Tracy told reporters. “Nothing new other than just, over the next couple of days, they’ll work on treatment, on getting the swelling out. See if he can get grip strength back, and then we’ll go from there. Just day to day.”
Tracy didn’t write off Contreras returning to the lineup this weekend.
“Never want to rule it out,” he said. “You get the swelling out of there and he could turn a corner really quickly. Just hard to say.”

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras was left furious after a 92.3 mph sinker drilled his right hand and forced him out of Thursday’s game. Just four days removed from a 10-day IL stint, Boston’s hitting leader was back screaming in pain at the plate, leaving Red Sox fans fearing the worst. But while Boston held its breath over another injury scare, former MLB catcher Erik Kratz had little sympathy.
“This picture right here with a line on the inside of the plate, this is why he’s getting hit. There are plenty of dudes that get hit. There are plenty of dudes that stand close to the plate that get hit and cry less than Willson,” Kratz said via Foul Territory.
“Starling Marte is up there. Freddie Freeman is up there. When and how many times do we hear those guys complaining about it? Anthony Rizzo was this guy. Rarely was there like, ‘Ooh, we gotta have retaliation.’ When you’re close to the plate, you’re gonna get hit. That’s the reality of it, but he’s taking exception to it. It’s also kind of a ploy. Get that ball out over the plate where I can do some damage.”
The only relief for Contreras was that X-rays came back negative. But with only eight regular-season games left, even a short absence from Boston’s best hitter is bad timing.
Thursday’s plunk was already his 24th of 2026, and Kratz is not buying the idea that this is simply bad luck.
Contreras crowds the plate. That is the point.
“If he’s concerned about getting hit in the hand, he can’t sit out over the plate looking for breaking balls and then all of a sudden the heater that doesn’t break catches him on the hand,” Kratz said.
He did not dismiss the danger, either. Kratz admitted the pitch could have been an “absolute death play” if it had broken Contreras’ hand. But his larger point was that Contreras knowingly puts himself in that position.
Contreras pushed back on that explanation.
“A lot of people might say that I hit on top of the plate. But I’m seeing a lot of players hit on top of the plate. They don’t get hit like me,” he said.
Kratz pointed to Freddie Freeman, Starling Marte, and Anthony Rizzo as the counterargument.
“Freddie Freeman is up there. How many times do we hear those guys complaining about it? Anthony Rizzo was this guy. Rarely was there like, ‘Oh, we gotta have retaliation.’”
Jose Altuve offers the opposite comparison. He stands farther off the plate and has been hit just three times this season and 83 times in 16 years. Contreras, meanwhile, is already at 24 HBPs in 2026 after recording 13 in 2023 and 12 in 2024.
Kratz boiled his criticism down even further.
“When you’re close to the plate, you’re going to get hit. That’s the reality of it.”
He also suggested there is another layer to Contreras’ setup.
“It’s also kind of a ploy. Get that ball out over the plate where I can do some damage.”
That is why Kratz sees this less as a Red Sox pitching problem and more as a trade-off Contreras accepts every time he steps into the box. The stance gives him access to pitches away, but it also leaves almost no room when pitchers challenge him inside.
And retaliation would not change that. Boston could answer by hitting someone back, but Contreras would still return to the same spot in the box.
For Kratz, this is not something the Red Sox pitching staff can solve for him. Contreras chose the setup, and the bruises come with it.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Tampa Bay Rays have been the best team in the American League for much of this season, particularly at Tropicana Field.
But with one All-Star on the injured list and two others unavailable, the Red Sox came away with a 4-2 victory before a crowd of 23,342 as Roman Anthony drove in three runs.
Now the magic number to clinch a playoff spot is down to two.
Ranger Suarez (8-4) and three relievers walked nine but held the Rays to five hits. Tampa Bay was hitless in 13 at-bats with runners in scoring position and left 12 men on base.
It was an impressive victory for the Sox, considering the 93-60 Rays are close to clinching the best record in the league and home-field advantage through, at least, the American League Championship Series.
The Sox were without Ceddanne Rafaela, who isn’t expected to come off the injured list until next week. Aroldis Chapman (lat strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) were not available.
With Garrett Whitlock left in the bullpen after pitching Thursday night, the Sox used lefthander Erik Miller to get the final three outs for his first save with the team.
Miller walked two and threw three wild pitches in a wild ninth inning, giving up a run before finally getting Chandler Simpson to ground to second for the final out.
Miller had allowed five runs over 5⅓ innings and put 10 men on base in his previous six appearances.
The Sox didn’t arrive at the team hotel until close to 5 a.m. after beating the Rangers in Texas on Thursday night. The Rays had a day game at home that ended 13 hours earlier. But the Sox had more energy early on.
Anthony blasted the third pitch of the game from Ian Seymour 438 feet to center field for his fifth home run.
Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the second inning with singles. Isiah Kiner-Falefa dropped a bunt to advance the runners before Nate Eaton worked a walk to load the bases.
After Connor Wong struck out, Anthony worked the count full and lined a hard single to right field to drive in two more runs. The three RBIs matched his career high.
Jahmai Jones homered leading off the third inning, a 414-foot shot to left field.
Suarez did not handle the run support very well. He walked a hitter in each of the first four innings and threw 69 pitches. But the Rays scored only one run.
Yandy Diaz walked leading off the bottom of the first, advanced to third on a double by Jonathan Aranda, and scored on Junior Caminero’s groundout.
Suarez was done after 5⅔ innings and 98 pitches, leaving the game with a runner at second. Wyatt Olds walked Liam Hicks and Victor Mesa Jr. on 12 pitches to load the bases.
He fell behind Jake Fraley 3 and 1, then came back to strike him out swinging through a fastball at the top of the strike zone. Olds threw up his hands after finally ending the inning. It wasn’t an elegant outing, but it was ultimately an effective one.
Greg Weissert worked around a two-out double by Caminero in the seventh inning to keep the lead at three runs, then came back for a 1-2-3 eighth.

Red Sox Insert Jahmai Jones into Lineup Against Rays Lefty
The Boston Red Sox placed designated hitter Jahmai Jones in the third spot in the starting lineup on Friday against Tampa Bay Rays left-hander Ian Seymour at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.
According to MLB.com, Jones sits in the heart of the order between outfielders Roman Anthony and Wilyer Abreu. Shortstop Trevor Story and first baseman Nick Sogard also feature in the top five positions for Boston.
Left-hander Ranger Suárez gets the start on the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay's Seymour. Seymour enters the contest holding a 9-6 record with a 4.27 ERA and 150 strikeouts on the season, according to official team statistics.
Boston manager Chad Tracy opted to stack the right-handed hitting Jones near the top of the batting order due to ongoing injuries and lack of availability among several key players, including Ceddanne Rafaela, Masataka Yoshida, Curtis Mead, and Willson Contreras.
According to MLB Trade Rumors, Boston acquired Jones off waivers on July 14 after the Detroit Tigers designated him for assignment, sending pitching prospect Jojo Ingrassia to Detroit as compensation.
Jones struggled with Detroit this season, batting .137 with a .221 slugging percentage across 105 plate appearances before his release. However, he has turned his season around in Boston, slashing .362/.464/.681 with three home runs and eight RBIs in 56 plate appearances.
Friday marks the 20th time overall this season that Jones has occupied the third spot in a starting lineup, having done so 19 times prior across his stints with Detroit and Boston. In those previous 35 plate appearances in the third spot, he posted a .219 batting average and a .661 OPS.
According to FanGraphs, the platoon splits support Boston's heavy usage of Jones against left-handed pitching. Across 138 plate appearances against lefties this year, Jones has recorded a .223 batting average, a .333 on-base percentage, and a .420 slugging percentage with five home runs, 15 walks, and 14 RBIs.
Conversely, Jones has registered just a .130 average in 23 at-bats against right-handed pitchers, with all five of his home runs this season coming exclusively against left-handers. He previously hit a two-run home run off Seymour during a July 18 matchup at Fenway Park.
Boston enters the three-game series against the American League East-leading Rays with an 83-70 record, holding the second AL Wild Card position and a five-game lead over the Cleveland Guardians. NESN reports Boston's magic number to clinch a postseason berth stands at three with nine games remaining on their schedule.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG – As they head into the final 10 days of the regular season, the Red Sox are monitoring a plethora of injuries to key players.
Given that the Sox still hold firm possession of the second American League Wild Card spot and could clinch a berth as early as this weekend, the plan will be to operate conservatively in hopes of getting everyone healthy for the games that count the most.
Here is an update on where things stand with those key players.
First baseman Willson Contreras
There was a big scare on Thursday night in Texas when the team’s most productive hitter this season was pelted on the top of his right hand with a pitch in the top of the eighth and immediately exited the game. Contreras said that in the moment, it felt like a fracture. Fortunately, X-rays taken at the ballpark were negative.
While interim manager Chad Tracy mentioned the possibility of follow-up imaging, there was none on Friday. Contreras didn’t have his hand taped and spent his share of time in the training room.
Where do things stand?
“Obviously, sore with some swelling,” Tracy said. “So nothing new other than just over the next couple of days, they'll work on treatment, on getting the swelling out, see if he can get grip strength back, and then we'll go from there. So just day to day.”
Could there still be additional scans?
“Not right now. Right now, with the initial one, they're optimistic,” said Tracy. “Just work on the swelling and see how he progresses over the next couple days, and then determine if they feel like they need more. But right now, they're just going to work on that.”
Closer Aroldis Chapman
When Garrett Whitlock closed Thursday’s win in Texas, it was obvious something was up with Chapman. It turns out he has been dealing with lat tightness he sustained while working out prior to Tuesday’s game.
Chapman downplayed the injury on Friday, saying the team is being conservative and that he felt healthy enough to play catch before the opener of the three-game series against the Rays. The Red Sox told him not to.
The lefty fireballer said he won’t pitch this weekend, but he expects to return during the final homestand, which starts on Tuesday.
“I’m not worried at all,” Chapman said. “From the first time I felt it to today, I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time.“
It is all about being 100% for the first game of the playoffs on Sept. 29, right?
“Yeah, of course,” said Chapman. “A hundred percent.”
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela
Boston’s All-Star center fielder hasn’t played since Sept. 2 due to a right quad strain. It sounds unlikely he’ll be able to play in a rehab game for Triple-A Worcester because that season ends on Sunday. But Tracy is confident with where Rafaela is at.
“I think he got close to 90% of his acceleration yesterday,” said Tracy. “So not ready yet, but he's moving quickly in the right direction, which is good. If he doesn’t play [for Worcester], there is a goal of getting him some live at-bats of some kind. You know, like live BP-type at-bats of some kind, plus the Trajekt. The important thing is that the running piece keeps going in the right direction.”
Left-hander Garrett Crochet
Boston’s ace, who has been out since April 25 due to a left shoulder injury, is still racing against the clock to try to pitch in relief during the postseason. His next step will be on Saturday, when he throws his second up-and-down bullpen session of the week at Fenway Park.
For Crochet to have any shot at pitching at the start of the postseason, he would have to start facing hitters by next week.
“I would say we're to the point where these next five days or so are going to be pretty telling,” said Tracy. “How does the side go, and what can we do with him early next week? And that'll give us a better idea of the answer to that question.”
Right-hander Tanner Houck
The righty will make the fourth and final appearance of his Minor League rehab assignment when he throws roughly 50 pitches for Worcester on Saturday. It’s possible Houck will get a tuneup or two in regular-season action for the Red Sox next week, which could give the club a better gauge if he’s a possibility to pitch in the playoffs. Houck had Tommy John surgery 13 months ago.

Willson Contreras played a key role in the Boston Red Sox's come-from-behind win in the series finale against the Texas Rangers, but not in a way he would have preferred. Contreras was plunked in the hand by struggling Rangers reliever Jakob Junis in the top of the eighth, setting the scene for Trevor Story to launch a go-ahead three-run homer off All-Star closer Jacob Latz.
The good news is that Contreras underwent x-rays following the game, and they came back clean. The veteran didn't seem to agree with the diagnosis, saying that it felt like a fracture and that he's fractured that hand before and experienced some numbness. More importantly, he's frustrated.
“If nobody does anything about it, I’m going to keep getting hit. That’s the way I see it. That’s it,” Contreras said, via Tim Healey of The Boston Globe.
Contreras has been hit by a pitch 24 times this season, third-most in the league. Of course, he also crowds the plate more than almost any hitter in the game. You want to claim the entire plate as your own; expect opposing pitchers to try and prove to you that the inside corner is, in fact, theirs.
By the sound of it, that is lost on Contreras. It seems as if the former St. Louis Cardinal wants one of Boston's pitchers to go out and start beaning batters in retaliation. That might be how things were done in the olden days, but now that's a recipe for escalation, a potential brawl, and possible suspensions.
Given that he doesn't feel as if any of the hurlers have come to his defense, it's likely that won't change. These bad feelings could become a cause for concern, and even more so with us approaching October's doorstep.
Willson Contreras could be threatening Red Sox chemistry again with latest HBP outrage
On the field, Contreras has had a fantastic first season in Boston. His 27 homers are already a career high, and if it holds, his .387 on-base percentage will be a career-best, too. Meanwhile, his .518 slugging percentage is the second-best mark of his career. There was a reason why he was voted a top AL MVP contender in an MLB.com poll at the end of August.
That's been great, but there have been issues. Contreras made some confusing comments after Alex Cora was dismissed, seemingly taking a shot at the team's young players in the process. He has also gotten into it with fans after being booed for not running out a ground ball back in August, further cementing his reputation as a prickly player.
At the same time, before the tide turned on the Red Sox's season and trade rumors enveloped him, he stated that he wouldn't waive his no-trade clause, desiring to finish his career in Boston.
Overall, it's odd. At times, it has seemed as if he doesn't really want to be here, despite his protest that, in fact, Boston is the only place he envisions himself playing.
This latest incident is more dangerous. Who knows what is said behind closed doors, but hurt bodies and hurt feelings don't go well together. If Contreras pushes the "defense" issue, it could cause a real rift. The pitchers could side with each other, while the hitters rally around Contreras.
The lines could also be different if there are enough players on either side of the positional divide with a more updated view of bean ball, so that different cliques could form.
The Red Sox have bigger issues at hand right now. They're going to have to figure out their postseason roster crunch. They're hoping that Aroldis Chapman's sore lat isn't anything serious. They need to find a way to get Roman Anthony's bat going before the playoffs begin. What they don't have time for is Contreras getting in his feelings because he got hit while standing on top of the plate.

The Boston Red Sox will not have Willson Contreras in the lineup on Friday night against the Tampa Bay Rays, but there is hope for the All-Star slugger after an early exit on Thursday night.
Contreras had to leave the club's series finale against the Texas Rangers on Thursday night after getting hit by a pitch on his hand. At the time, it was reported that his X-rays came back negative, but there was still some fear. Contreras himself spoke about the injury and said that it felt like a fracture while citing the fact that he previously had one.
Now, of course, it would've been great to see Contreras in Boston's lineup on Friday, but he hasn't been ruled out for the weekend and Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy shared that no new scans are currently planned, as shared on X by MassLive.com's Sean McAdam.
Willson Contreras Update
"Willson Contreras is out of the lineup, giving his hand some time to recover. Chad Tracy wouldn’t rule him out for the weekend, but Sox are being cautious. No new scans planned," McAdam wrote on X.
Again, it would've been great to see Contreras back in the lineup, but there are positives to take away from this update. First and foremost, the fact that more scans aren't currently planned is a sign of confidence from the club. Think back to Curtis Mead, for example. When he got hit on the wrist in his first game as a member of the Red Sox, his X-rays initially came back as negative. Then, the next day, it was shared that he actually had suffered a fractured wrist.
At this point, every time someone gets hit by a pitch on the wrist/hand, it immediately makes fans think about Mead. This process with Contreras is much more positive than it was with Mead. The fact that almost 24 hours later, the club hasn't ruled him out for the weekend and doesn't have more tests planned is a very good sign that he simply is dealing with a bruise, or something of that nature.
Boston needs Contreras if it wants to make a run this season. Things are wide open in the American League, especially in the wake of Aaron Judge being placed on the Injured List for the New York Yankees. Boston, New York and Tampa Bay are the top three contenders in the American League and with New York hurting, the top two contenders should be the Red Sox and the Rays. If Contreras returns over the weekend, Boston is going to be just fine.

Boston Red Sox fans were already going through it on Thursday night after Willson Contreras left the series finale against the Texas Rangers early after being hit by a pitch on the hand. Seeing Garrett Whitlock emerge from the bullpen to close a 4-3 game in the ninth inning only made fears worse.
Whitlock is no slouch, as Red Sox fans know, and he got through the ninth frame unscathed, but fans expect to see Aroldis Chapman in moments like that. After the game, Boston announced that Chapman was unavailable due to a lat issue.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said in his September 17 postgame presser that Chapman has been dealing with lat tightness for a couple of days but that he's been improving lately. Boston has classified him as day-to-day and it will routinely check on his recovery progress to gauge his availability.
The best news from Tracy on Chapman is that the team will not place him on the injured list. The Sox's bullpen has been one of their deadliest weapons all season and Chapman with his 1.95 ERA, 34 saves, blistering velocity and unmatched consistency at 38 years old has been a huge part of that success.
Aroldis Chapman injury news is a blow the Red Sox's bullpen can't afford as the playoffs near
Still, having Chapman at anything less than 100 percent is dangerous this late in the season with the playoffs on the horizon. In a tight game, one slip-up in the ninth inning could lead to disaster.
The rest of the Red Sox's bullpen is hardly in its best shape. Justin Slaten's season ended following continued flexor issues and Tyron Guerrero is still on the IL bouncing back from shoulder inflammation. Erik Miller is also dealing with a mechanical issue that has severely impacted his command over his last two outings.
If Chapman's injury is as mild as Tracy is letting on and he doesn't need an IL stint, Boston might be able to avoid disaster. But it also needs Chapman's help to clinch its playoff spot in the first place. The offense is struggling to get out to enough of a lead that it doesn't need Chapman to hold a slim margin in the late innings, but that won't fly in the postseason, especially with an injured closer.
At least the Red Sox expect some relief reinforcements in the coming days. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working towards returns from long-term injuries in a relief role and they could take some pressure off the 'pen, but neither could fill Chapman's role.

The Boston Red Sox seem to be stalling out at the worst possible time. The offense has had trouble limiting strikeouts, advancing runners and hitting, in general with a clinching opportunity on the line.
But under the doom and gloom of the rest of the offense, there is hidden a triumphant return from injury by an unexpected player: Trevor Story. He played hero on September 17 against the Texas Rangers with an eighth-inning, three-run homer to stave off a sweep and help his team inch closer to clinching a playoff berth.
Even before that, Story had been hitting well while the rest of Boston's bats have faltered, including some of its best, like Willson Contreras and Roman Anthony (subscription required). Story is slashing .349/.359/.508 with seven doubles, a home run and nine RBI since he returned from the injured list on August 30. Boston's lineup hasn't been long enough lately to make the best of its minimal offensive production, so Story's efforts have gone under-the-radar.
There's quite a bit of swing and miss in Story's game, as there always has been. He's fanned at a 31.3 percent clip in the 16 games he's played since coming off the IL, which hasn't helped Boston's strikeout totals each game. But Story got the job done when the Sox needed him most, and for that he deserves credit.
Trevor Story has been a bright spot in Red Sox's offense throughout September slump
The Red Sox have looked utterly lifeless at the plate and Story was able to break through the ugly spell. With any luck, his game-saver from Thursday night will inspire his teammates to free themselves from whatever late-season funk they're in, which has delayed their clinching ceremony enough already.
It's reassuring to see Story get hot with just a few series remaining. He also performed exceptionally well last September with a .302/.337/.458 slash line, six doubles, three home runs and 12 RBI over 22 games that month. He's looking like a weapon en-route to a Wild Card matchup for the second year in a row.
Story has also seemingly crushed the slump he was in when the season started. The shortstop batted only .206/.244/.303 with 57 strikeouts to just eight walks over 41 games before his injury. Before Story and the Red Sox revealed the sports hernia bugging the infielder, fans were under the impression that another rough year was coming, but pain from the injury might've severely hampered his play.
After Boston went without signing a true slugger over the offseason (a Pete Alonso or Kyle Schwarber type, a more consistent home run hitter than Contreras), it needed Story to build off his 2025 season for the offense to be at its best. There hasn't been much power in Story's game yet, but maybe his game-saving homer against the Rangers changes the tides. Story has been one of few bright spots this month in the Red Sox's underachieving offense and the rest of the team needs to play closer to his level to maintain its Wild Card standing as the regular season draws to a close.

ARLINGTON, Texas — Trevor Story, who is from Irving, hit a go-ahead, three-run home run off Jacob Latz in the eighth inning Thursday night. The Boston Red Sox beat the Texas Rangers, 4-3, at Globe Life Field and kept Texas from a three-game sweep.
The Colorado Rockies drafted Story 45th overall in 2011 out of Irving High School, where he hit .488 as a senior. He had committed to LSU.
Boston trailed 3-1 entering the eighth. Story reached down for Latz’s second straight low curveball, an 80.3 mph pitch, and lined it over the wall in left-center field. It was his fourth home run of the season and his first since May 13. The loss dropped Texas one game behind the Houston Astros in the AL West.
The challenges of the year were part of it for Story.
“It meant a lot,” Story said. “Just the challenges of the year and all that, but just trying to be present in the moment to help the team win. And today was a good one, that was fun.”
Trevor Story Has A Hit in 15 Of 16 Games Since Sports Hernia Surgery
Boston placed Story on the 10-day injured list May 16 with a sports hernia that had bothered him since the spring. He had surgery later that month and was transferred to the 60-day IL on June 4. Since returning Aug. 30, Story has a hit in all but one of his 16 games, and he is riding an eight-game hitting streak. He is slashing .327/.339/.473 in September.
Story tries to use the outside noise in a way that fits him.
“It’s tough because I’m not really motivated by outside noise or anything,” Story explained. “But you hear it, and I try to use it in a way that fits me best. Like we said, that was the point of getting the surgery, to come back and try to be the player that I know I can be, and I’m starting to show that.”
Chad Tracy Says Trevor Story Delivered ‘A Massive Swing’
Jakob Junis set up the at-bat by walking Wilyer Abreu and hitting Willson Contreras to open the eighth. Latz then struck out Adley Rutschman. Story had just missed Latz’s fastball a couple of times earlier in the at-bat.
“I was looking for something just to put in play,” Story said. “[Latz has] a good fastball and just missed it a couple times, and I felt good about that. Just trying to get something in the zone and get on top of it, and was able to drive one out.”
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said he saw Story change games that way numerous times in the second half of last season.
“He’s been great,” Tracy said. “He’s got a hit in every game but one. That was a hell of an at-bat against a really good pitcher in a really big spot and a huge swing. Obviously needed a win, but all the credit to him.”
“You’re one pitch away in a spot like that, where he can change a game, like we saw it numerous times in the second half of last year,” Tracy continued. “So, like I said, it was a massive swing.”
Boston (83-70) holds the second AL Wild Card spot, five games ahead of the Cleveland Guardians. The Red Sox open a three-game series against the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday and could clinch a postseason berth there.

As the regular season winds down, the Red Sox will have to manage their injuries in their pursuit of a deep October run. They open their weekend series against the red-hot Rays in Tampa on Friday night, possibly without their most consistent hitter.
Contreras said he probably won't play in the series opener.
Contreras told the Boston Globe he originally felt like he had fractured his hand, an injury he's experienced before.
"Sore. Painful. My hand was numb for like five minutes," Contreras said. "That was the reason I came out of the game. I have fractured, before, the same hand. It felt like a fracture. Thankfully, it's not a fracture on the top of the bone."
Contreras also expressed frustration over being frequently hit by pitches during his time in the big leagues. This season, Contreras ranks third in the majors in hit-by-pitches.
"If nobody does anything about it, I'm going to keep getting hit. That's the way I see it. That's it," he explained.
"I mean, sore bones in the hands — might take two days, might take a week, might take ten days. I don't know. We'll see how I feel after taking this plane to Tampa."
Should the Rays come out on top of the AL East, the Red Sox will likely face the Yankees in the AL Wild Card series, one in which they'll need their best hitters at 100% against one of the top pitching staffs in the league.

Willson Contreras gets hit by a lot of pitches — he's been hit 24 times in 129 games this year, tying his career high — but the one on September 17 was different. Contreras mostly takes his base without issue, occasionally chirping pitchers and trying to rally his teammates on the way, but it was obvious something was wrong this time.
In the top of the eighth inning, a pitch from Texas Rangers pitcher Jakob Junis knocked Contreras in the hand. The first baseman hit the ground and immediately shook out his hand in pain. He walked off the field with a trainer uncharacteristically fast, which only worsened fans' nerves.
Postgame x-rays of Contreras' hand came back clear of any breaks but he's still experiencing pain (according to Chris Cotillo of MassLive). Contreras is less convinced by the results of the imaging. He told reporters he thinks his hand is fractured and that it went numb for a time after the hit (via Tim Healey of The Boston Globe).
The Red Sox have classified Contreras as day-to-day, but his reaction coupled with the club's history of evaluating injuries has some people doubting the diagnosis. The situation is reminiscent of what happened with Curtis Mead.
Willson Contreras' pain level seemingly outweighing initial diagnosis is giving Red Sox fans Curtis Mead flashbacks
A pitch plunked Mead on the wrist in his second at-bat as a Red Sox following the team's acquisition at the trade deadline. Initial imaging came back clear. The following day, he underwent a more detailed scan that revealed a wrist fracture. The fracture was non-displaced, meaning the broken part of his wrist remained aligned so he didn't have to undergo surgery to repair it, but his wrist is fractured all the same.
The Red Sox had better hope their initial diagnosis is correct this time. Losing Contreras for any amount of time, even with a day-to-day diagnosis, is a brutal outcome for the Sox. He's fresh off the injured list after a nearly two-week stint with a hamstring issue and he expects to be sidelined again for at least a few days.
Contreras has been Boston's most important bat all season and his career-high 27 home runs lead the team. The Red Sox need Contreras at his best for their playoff run, but if his hand is injured in any way, "his best" may be out the window.
Hopefully Contreras' initial diagnosis is right and Boston doesn't have another Mead situation on its hands. Contreras has been too important to the Red Sox's offense all season and his leadership is too valuable to lose him long-term at such a critical time, but the injury bug doesn't bite at ideal times.
